newsitem.title: USA: Las Cruces, N.M., plans to build power substation.
newsitem.headline: Las Cruces, N.M., plans to build power substation.

text.p: The city of Las Cruces, New Mexico, announced this week plans to construct a new substation and distribution network to serve an industrial park as it continues to pursue purchase of an existing distribution system from El Paso Electric Co.
Las Cruces spokesman Christopher Good said Friday a key tenant of the West Mesa park made re-location to the city contingent on lower electricity rates.
"El Paso Electric is currently supplying our power. We could wait for them to build the new facilities or we could build it ourselves," he said.
But Henry Quintana, spokesman for El Paso Electric, said the utility would be able to serve additional customers with existing facilities.
Las Cruces has been trying to establish a municipal utility since the early 1990's, but El Paso has resisted sale of its distribution lines.
Last week, New Mexico Governor Gary Johnson signed legislation granting Las Cruces the right to appropriate the distribution system from El Paso.
Previously, the issue was tied up in court.
Las Cruces plans to purchase power from a neighboring utility, Southwestern Public Service Co, for about 20 percent less than El Paso's rates, Good said.
The city has also filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) for clarification of whether it owes any money to El Paso for recovery of stranded costs.
Las Cruces maintains that El Paso's financial difficulties - it emerged from bankruptcy last year - stem from its 15.8 percent equity stake in the Palo Verde nuclear plant in Arizona.
The city had officially opposed the nuclear investment, noted Good.
"But Palo Verde is there and has been supplying power to the city of Las Cruces," said Quintana at El Paso.
El Paso estimates stranded costs of up to $200 million associated with the distribution lines, on top of a market value near $130 million, he noted.
"We expect them to file a condemnation procedure, but the question is do they have enough money to buy it (the distribution system)," Quintana said.
Las Cruces has said it would not pursue municipalization if the lines cost more than $90 million, he added.
